title: Privilege Escalation
summary: Privilege escalation is the set of actions that convert ordinary user or service access into authority the account was never intended to hold, whether that means higher rights on the same host or rights that reach across a domain or cloud tenant. Vertical escalation raises the level of permission an identity holds, while horizontal escalation moves to a different identity with comparable rights and is often a stepping stone rather than an end in itself. The underlying causes are consistent across platforms: excessive standing privilege, misconfigured permissions on files, services or container runtimes, unpatched local software, credential material left in memory, configuration files or environment variables, and trust relationships that let a low-trust principal assume a high-trust role. Cloud and container estates add their own variants, including over-broad role assumption policies, instance metadata reachable from a workload, and container configurations that expose the host. Because escalation usually abuses legitimate functionality, signature-based detection alone is inadequate. Useful signals include process trees in which a user-facing application spawns a shell or administrative utility, changes to local or directory group membership, newly granted roles or permissions, and access to privileged interfaces outside a change window. Effective mitigation is architectural rather than detective: least privilege, removal of standing administrative rights in favour of just-in-time elevation, unique local administrator credentials, timely patching, and application control that limits what an unprivileged user can execute. Detection then concentrates on the residual cases where those controls fail or are bypassed.
objectives: You will be able to distinguish vertical from horizontal privilege escalation and give a realistic example of each.
You will be able to identify the misconfiguration classes that most often enable escalation on hosts, directories and cloud tenants.
You will be able to read process ancestry and permission-change telemetry to recognise escalation behaviour.
You will be able to prioritise privilege reduction using standing rights, administrative tiering and just-in-time access.
You will be able to explain how container configuration and instance metadata exposure change the escalation picture.
